To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TP53 mutations are frequent in TCC of the urinary bladder, but TP53 accumulation occurs frequently in the presence of a wild-type TP53 gene.

TP53 mutations were present in 33% of TCC of the urinary bladder, that the mutations were clustered in exons 6-9, and that TP53 accumulation was associated with poor prognosis, but was not necessarily due to TP53 mutations.
TP53 nuclear accumulation in more than 5% of the tumour cell nuclei is a frequent event in transitional cell carcinoma of urinary bladder, and is associated with poor survival.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of TP53 mutations and TP53 protein accumulation in the development of human bladder cancer.
the development of a new method for the study of tumour-suppressor genes, which may be applicable to a wide range of tumours.

the molecular genetic alterations of TP53 gene in human urinary bladder transitional cell carcinoma (TCCT) and the relationship of these alterations with the clinicopathologic parameters and patient survival.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TP53 mutations in bladder TCC are associated with a poor prognosis.

mutations of the TP53 gene are not the only molecular events that lead to accumulation of the protein, and that the presence of TP533 in the absence of TP53 mutations is also associated with poor patient prognosis.

the presence of TP533 mutations and/or accumulation of TP53 protein in the majority of tumour cell populations is associated with a worse prognosis in TCC of the bladder, but that TP53 mutations alone are not necessarily associated with an unfavourable prognosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TP53 accumulation is a frequent event in bladder tumours, and that the presence of mutations in TP53 is associated with poor survival.

the TP53 gene is mutated in a significant proportion of TCC of the human urinary tract, and that the presence of TP533 mutations and the accumulation of TP53 protein are both associated with poor prognosis, although the accumulation of TP533 in more than 20% of tumour nuclei may be a more important predictor of prognosis than the presence of TP33 mutations.

(a) TP53 mutation is not a prerequisite for TP53 nuclear reactivation in TCC, but that the majority of TP53 mutations occur in exons 5-9; (b) the presence of TP 53 nuclear reactivity (in > 50% tumour cell nuclei) is a significant indicator of poor prognosis in patients with TCC of the human urinary tract.
The main takeaway from our work is that
immunohistochemistry is an important tool to assess the status of TP53, and that it should be performed on paraffin sections of tumour tissue.
immunohistochemistry is a useful and practical approach for the detection of TP53 accumulation and its prognostic significance in TCC.
immunohistochemistry for TP53 is a useful prognostic marker, and can be used to select patients for TP53 mutation analysis.
